ai.definition: Gene-edited xenotransplantation involves transplanting organs from genetically modified pigs into humans to address the severe shortage of donor organs.
ai.howItWorks: Donor pigs undergo extensive gene editing to remove pig-specific antigens and retroviruses, and to add human compatibility genes. The edited organs are then transplanted into recipients who are closely monitored for immune reactions and other complications.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the chronic shortage of donor organs by using genetically modified pig organs as a viable alternative.
ai.manufacturing: The process involves complex genetic engineering techniques to modify pigs, followed by organ harvesting and preservation before transplantation.
ai.buildProcess: Pigs are bred in controlled environments where their genes are edited using CRISPR or other gene-editing technologies. The organs are then harvested under sterile conditions and stored for transplantation.
ai.costDrivers: High costs associated with genetic modification, organ harvesting, storage, and the intensive monitoring required post-transplantation.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in clinical trials and moving towards broader application as safety and efficacy are demonstrated.
ai.regulation: Subject to stringent regulatory oversight due to potential biosecurity risks and ethical considerations, requiring approval from multiple agencies before widespread use.
ai.risks: Potential for immune rejection, transmission of viruses, and long-term health effects on recipients.
ai.profitability: Uncertain at this stage; profitability will depend on the success rate of clinical trials, regulatory approvals, and market demand for alternative organ sources.
ai.futureDevelopment: Continued research to improve genetic modifications, reduce immunogenicity, and enhance long-term outcomes. Exploration of additional applications beyond kidney and heart transplantation.

subsystems.name: Gene editing platform
subsystems.role: rewrites the pig genome so human immune systems tolerate the organ.

buildSteps.title: Choose and edit the genes
buildSteps.detail: Researchers select edits that remove pig surface sugars (such as alpha-gal and CMAH) and inactivate porcine endogenous retroviruses, while adding human complement-regulatory and anticoagulant genes.

buildSteps.title: Create founder pigs
buildSteps.detail: Edited pig cells are fused with eggs and implanted into surrogate sows, producing piglets that carry the edits. These founders are bred to establish stable lines.

buildSteps.title: Raise a biosecure herd
buildSteps.detail: The pigs are kept in filtered, restricted-access facilities, tested repeatedly for viruses and bacteria, and monitored for genetic drift.

buildSteps.title: Harvest the organ
buildSteps.detail: At a set age and weight, the donor pig is anaesthetised and the organ is removed under sterile conditions, then flushed and cooled or placed on a perfusion machine.

buildSteps.title: Transplant into the recipient
buildSteps.detail: Surgeons connect the organ to the patient's blood vessels and, for a kidney, to the urinary tract, usually alongside the patient's own failing organ.

buildSteps.title: Suppress and monitor the immune response
buildSteps.detail: The patient receives immunosuppressive drugs and is monitored closely for signs of rejection through blood tests and biopsies.

buildSteps.title: Track infection and organ function
buildSteps.detail: Frequent testing looks for pig viruses, and imaging and blood work track how well the organ works over weeks and months.

buildSteps.title: Follow up for life
buildSteps.detail: Recipients are enrolled in long-term registries to watch for delayed rejection, infections, or other complications.
